title: You alright?
description: Hello; how are you?
details:
Example: Morning! You alright?

Usage: Informal British greeting. It can also be a real welfare check, depending on tone and context.

title: Cheers
description: Thanks.
details:
Example: Cheers for the lift.

Usage: Informal; also used when making a toast. Here it expresses thanks.

title: No worries
description: That’s okay; it isn’t a problem.
details:
Example: Sorry I’m late. No worries.

Usage: An informal reply to an apology or thanks; also used outside Britain.

title: Not to worry
description: There’s no need to be concerned.
details:
Example: Not to worry. We can catch the next bus.

Usage: A reassuring response to a small problem.

title: Fancy a cuppa?
description: Would you like a cup of tea?
details:
Example: I’m putting the kettle on. Fancy a cuppa?

Usage: Informal British English; cuppa usually means a cup of tea.

title: I’ll put the kettle on
description: I’ll boil water, usually to make tea or coffee.
details:
Example: Come in. I’ll put the kettle on.

Usage: Often serves as an informal offer of a hot drink.

title: Give me a shout
description: Let me know or ask me when you need something.
details:
Example: Give me a shout if you need a hand.

Usage: Informal; it needn’t involve actually shouting.

title: I’ll pop in
description: I’ll make a short visit.
details:
Example: I’ll pop in after work.

Usage: Pop round is another informal British way to describe a short visit to someone’s home.

title: I’ll be a minute
description: I’ll be ready or back very soon.
details:
Example: I’m just finding my keys. I’ll be a minute.

Usage: Informal; usually means a short time, not exactly sixty seconds.

title: I’m just having a look
description: I’m browsing and don’t need help yet.
details:
Example: Can I help you? Thanks, I’m just having a look.

Usage: A polite response to staff when browsing in a shop.

title: Takeaway
description: Food bought from a restaurant to eat elsewhere.
details:
Example: Shall we get a takeaway tonight?

Usage: British usage; American English commonly uses takeout.

title: Is that to eat in?
description: Will you eat the food here?
details:
Example: Is that to eat in or take away?

Usage: A question staff may ask. A customer can answer To eat in, please.

title: I can’t be bothered
description: I don’t want to make the effort.
details:
Example: I can’t be bothered to cook tonight.

Usage: Informal; can sound dismissive if used about helping someone or doing your job.

title: I’m shattered
description: I’m extremely tired.
details:
Example: I’m shattered. I’m going to bed.

Usage: Informal British English; use tired in a more neutral situation.

title: That’s a bit pricey
description: That seems quite expensive.
details:
Example: Twenty pounds for lunch? That’s a bit pricey.

Usage: Informal; a mild complaint about cost.

title: It’s a bit of a pain
description: It’s inconvenient or annoying.
details:
Example: Changing trains twice is a bit of a pain.

Usage: Informal; here pain describes inconvenience, not physical pain.

title: I’m not feeling great
description: I feel a little unwell or low.
details:
Example: I’m not feeling great, so I’m staying home.

Usage: Can refer to physical health or mood; add detail if needed.

title: I’ll sort it out
description: I’ll deal with the problem or arrangement.
details:
Example: The booking’s wrong. I’ll sort it out.

Usage: Informal; a promise to handle something.

title: Have you got…?
description: Do you have something?
details:
Example: Have you got a spare pen?

Usage: A natural British way to ask about possession or availability.

title: I’ll leave you to it
description: I’ll let you continue what you were doing.
details:
Example: You look busy. I’ll leave you to it.

Usage: A friendly way to finish a chat or stop interrupting someone.
